system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2178-08-23 19:18:00 to 2178-08-24 19:17:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for placement of a Dobhoff feeding tube and replacement of his tunneled central line due to malnutrition and ongoing treprostinil therapy for portopulmonary hypertension. He reported significant anorexia and weight loss attributed to treprostinil, despite using megestrol to improve appetite. A tunneled line was successfully placed on hospital day two, and a Dobhoff tube was inserted endoscopically the following day, with radiographic confirmation of correct placement. Tube feeds were initiated and tolerated well. Five liters of ascitic fluid were removed during paracentesis, with no signs of infection. His kidney function improved, with creatinine normalizing, and liver enzymes remained stable. He was discharged home with services to continue tube feeds, treprostinil via the new line, and all home medications, including ciprofloxacin for SBP prophylaxis. Outpatient follow-up and lab monitoring were arranged.
problems: Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol

radiology_notes.text:
There is moderate compression of mid thoracic and mid to lower thoracic
vertebral bodies grossly stable compared to CT torso from ___. 
Also, not well assessed loss of height of a upper lumbar vertebral body again
seen.

HISTORY:  Shortness of breath after line placement.

TECHNIQUE:  Frontal lateral views of the chest.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:

Enteric tube is seen coursing below the diaphragm, distal aspect not included
on the image.  There are bibasilar and right middle lobe patchy opacities. 
Patient has reported chronic lung disease.  There is no pleural effusion or
pneumothorax.  The cardiac silhouette is not enlarged.  Mediastinal silhouette
is unremarkable.  Calcified left hilar nodes are seen.

IMPRESSION:

No pneumothorax.  Patchy basilar and right middle lobe opacities.  Left
basilar opacities may be chronic.  Right middle lobe opacity appears
increased, query acute (infection or aspiration) on chronic process or
worsening of known chronic lung disease.

INDICATION:   ___ year old man with pulmponary hypertension on Remodulin
treatment. Place right sided, single lumen tunneled line for Remodulin
infusion and calculate priming volume of the cathter after cut into final
length.

CLINICIANS:  Dr. ___ and Dr ___ (attending)
performed the procedure.

ANESTHESIA:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
fentanyl (100 mcg) and Versed (2 mg) throughout a total intraservice time of
35 minutes during which patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously
monitored. Local anesthesia was provided by 1% lidocaine to the dermis and 1%
lidocaine with epinephrine into the subcutaneous tissues along the tunnel.

PROCEDURE:  Written informed consent was obtained from the patient after
explaining the risks, benefits, alternatives and indications of the procedure.

The patient was transported to the angiography suite and placed supine on the
imaging table.  The right neck was prepped and draped in usual sterile
fashion. A preprocedure huddle and timeout was performed per ___ protocol.

After anesthetizing the skin and subcutaneous tissues a micropuncture needle
was inserted into the patent right internal jugular vein under ultrasound
guidance.  Ultrasound images were saved for reference.  A 0.018 nitinol wire
was advanced into the superior vena cava.  After additional anesthesia, a
small ___ was made in the skin.  Micropuncture needle was exchanged with
micropuncture sheath.  The inner cannula and nitinol wire were removed.  A
0.035 J-wire was advanced into the right atrium.  Appropriate measurements
were made for skin incision four fingerbreadths below the venotomy site. The
length of the tunneled catheter from skin entrance to the tip was determined,
and its priming volume was measured three times and confirmed to be 1 mL. The
wire was then advanced into the IVC for stabilty.

Attention was now turned to creation of subcutaneous tunnel.  After additional
local anesthesia a 3 mm skin incision was made.  A 9.5 ___ single lumen
tunneled catheter was passed from the incision to the venotomy site with aid
of metal tunneling device.  The venotomy tract was dilated with 7 and 9 ___
dilators. A ___ Peel-away sheath was passed over the wire.  The wire and inner
cannula were removed and the catheter was passed through the peel-away sheath.
The peel-away sheath was removed while the catheter was pushed into the right
atrium.  This was confirmed with fluoroscopy demonstrating the catheter tip in
the right atrium.  

The lumen withdrew blood and flushed easily.  The catheter was secured with 0
silk sutures.  Venotomy site was closed with 4 Vicryl subcuticular suture. Dry

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. I understand your line came out earlier today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it just fell out. I didn’t pull it or anything. I was worried because I haven’t had my remodulin in over three hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we restarted your remodulin through a temporary IV in your arm. You’re getting it now, so you’re not going without.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I hate going without it. Last time I did, I felt short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we need to replace your tunneled line quickly. The team is scheduling it for tonight. It’ll go back into your neck vein and end in your heart, just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be safe? My platelets are low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked that. Your platelet count is low due to your liver disease, and the blood bank says you don’t respond well to transfusions. So we’ll proceed carefully without one, since you’ve had procedures before without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s safe. And my back pain—can I still take my usual pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep your MS Contin and Dilaudid for breakthrough pain. The imaging shows your old compression fractures are stable, so we’ll manage it the same way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure is done. We placed the new tunneled line through your right internal jugular vein. The tip is in the right atrium, and it’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Is it safe to use right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We confirmed it flushes easily and draws blood. The priming volume is only 1 mL, so it’s efficient. You’ll go back to your home remodulin dose tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable—same as before. No signs of infection. We did a chest X-ray after the procedure to make sure there was no pneumothorax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some shortness of breath afterward. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray showed some patchy opacities in your lungs, likely from your chronic lung disease. No pneumonia or fluid. Your oxygen levels are good at 93% on room air, so we think it’s stable portopulmonary syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you today. You’ve already infused your home remodulin dose through the new line without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I manage it myself at home. No nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’re confident doing it. Just keep all your meds going—sildenafil, spironolactone, rifaximin, and the testosterone patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the diuretics for my belly swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, torsemide and spironolactone continue. Watch your weight—call if you gain more than three pounds in a day. And follow up with transplant clinic as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the dressing dry for 48 hours. After that, you can shower. Watch for redness, swelling, or fever—call us if those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your gabapentin and narcotics. The fractures are stable, so it’s chronic pain. We’ll address it at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better knowing the line is back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You can go home in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your scrotal swelling has increased a bit. It’s likely from fluid due to cirrhosis. Keep taking your diuretics and monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch it. Thanks for everything.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted after his tunneled central line spontaneously displaced, interrupting his continuous remodulin infusion for portopulmonary hypertension. He was stabilized with a peripheral IV remodulin infusion and underwent urgent placement of a new right internal jugular tunneled catheter, which was successfully implanted with the tip in the right atrium. He tolerated the procedure well without complications. His chronic conditions, including cirrhosis, ascites, thrombocytopenia, and vertebral compression fractures, remained stable. He resumed his home remodulin dose through the new line and was discharged home the following day with instructions to monitor weight, manage his line, and follow up with transplant clinic. No new infections or procedural complications occurred.
